title: Create, copy, move, delete — safely
objective: By the end of this lesson you can manage files from the command line, and you have working habits that stop the one mistake that ends careers.

blocks.text: The commands here are short and there are not many of them. The command line does what you typed, immediately. No confirmation, no recycle bin. That is the part to internalise before the commands themselves.

blocks.caption: The core set
lines: mkdir -p reports/2026/q3   # make the whole chain at once
touch notes.txt            # create an empty file
cp -r reports archive      # copy a directory and its contents
mv notes.txt final.txt     # rename (move within the same place)
rmdir empty-folder         # delete an empty directory

blocks.text: Looking inside a file without opening an editor

rows: The file is short and you want all of it
The file is long — scroll with arrows, q to quit
You only need the first 10 lines
You only need the last 10 lines
The file is being written to right now and you want to watch it live

blocks.title: tail -f is how you watch a system think
blocks.text: Run tail -f on a log file, then trigger the thing you are testing in another window. Watching entries appear while you reproduce a problem lets you tie an action to its effect.
The command that deserves its reputation

rm -rf means "delete this, everything inside it, recursively, and do not ask me about anything". It is useful, and it has destroyed production systems. There is no undo. The files are not in a bin somewhere.

blocks.title: The three habits that prevent the disaster
blocks.text: First: run ls with the same path before you run rm with it — look at exactly what is about to go. Second: never put a wildcard next to a slash you have not read twice; the space in `rm -rf / tmp/old` instead of `rm -rf /tmp/old` is a real and famous way to erase a machine. Third: on anything that matters, check pwd before deleting relative paths.

blocks.caption: The habit, written out
lines: ls -la /tmp/build-cache      # look first — is this really what I mean?

blocks.title: Why this is a security lesson, not just a safety one
blocks.text: Destroying data is an availability failure, and availability is one third of the security triad alongside confidentiality and integrity. An engineer who deletes the wrong directory has caused a security incident, whatever the intent was.

blocks.title: Practise in a throwaway directory
steps: Run: ls -R a          (see the structure you made)
Run: cp -r a a-copy   (copy the whole tree)
Run: ls -la a-copy    (look before you delete — always this order)
blocks.expected: You built a small tree, copied it, inspected the copy, and removed it. Practising the look-then-act order in a sandbox is how it becomes automatic when it matters.

cheatsheet: mkdir -p makes the whole path chain · touch creates an empty file
cp -r and mv work on directories; mv is also how you rename
cat short files · less long files · head/tail for the ends
tail -f watches a file live — the debugging workhorse
rm has no undo and no recycle bin
Always ls the exact path first, then rm it
Deleting the wrong data is an availability incident, not just a mistake

checkpoint.prompt: You want to watch new lines appear in a log file as they are written. What do you use?

choices.B: cat logfile in a second terminal

checkpoint.explanation: tail -f follows the file, printing new lines as they arrive. The others show a snapshot and return.

checkpoint.prompt: What is the habit that most reliably prevents deleting the wrong thing?

choices.B: Run ls on that path first
choices.D: Running rm twice to be sure

checkpoint.explanation: Look-then-act. Run ls on the exact same path and read the output — that shows you precisely what the command will affect, before it is irreversible.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is accidental deletion described as a security incident?

choices.A: It is not — it is only an operations problem
choices.B: Because it is always caused by an attacker
choices.C: Because availability is part of the security triad
choices.D: Because deleted files can be recovered by attackers

checkpoint.explanation: Security covers confidentiality, integrity and availability. Data that is gone is an availability failure regardless of whether anyone acted maliciously.
